lessons.title: The Three Flows, and Picking the Right One

items: Name the three auto layout flows and what each one does to its children
Predict what wrap produces in a horizontal versus a vertical flow
Choose between a wrapping flow and a grid for a given layout

reading.text: Auto layout is the mechanism that makes a layout respond to its contents instead of being positioned by hand. Without it you place objects at coordinates, and every change to the content means moving them again. With it you describe a relationship — these items sit in a row, eight pixels apart, with sixteen pixels of breathing room around them — and the layout recomputes itself when the content changes. That difference is the whole distinction between designing a screen and designing a system.

It is also the first thing to learn, because almost everything else depends on it. Components are reusable because their internals reflow. Variables for spacing are useful because something consumes them. A prototype transition looks right because the two frames it animates between are built the same way. Start here and the rest compounds; skip it and you will rebuild every file by hand.
Three flows

items: Vertical — children stack top to bottom.
Horizontal — children sit left to right.
Grid — children occupy cells in rows and columns.

reading.text: Figma guesses when you apply auto layout: it "will try to determine which auto layout flow ... you want to use." The guess is based on how the objects are already arranged, and it is frequently right, which is exactly why it is worth knowing that it is a guess. You can switch to a different flow at any time, and the layout will rearrange to match.
Wrap belongs to the flows, not to the grid

Horizontal and vertical flows can wrap: when the children no longer fit along the axis, they continue on a new line. A horizontal flow wraps into a new row — the behaviour you want for a tag list, a chip set, or a gallery of cards that should reflow as the frame narrows. A vertical flow wraps into a new column.
"Vertical wrap is not a masonry layout." A wrapped vertical flow fills one column, then starts the next. It does not pack items of differing heights into the shortest available slot.

That sentence exists in the documentation because the expectation is so common. Masonry is the Pinterest arrangement — ragged, height-packed, no visible rows. Vertical wrap produces columns. If you reach for it expecting masonry you will get something orderly and wrong, and you will spend an hour looking for the setting that fixes it. There isn't one.

reading.caption: The same six items, of differing heights, under three rules. A grid places them into cells, so rows align and a short item leaves space beneath it. Vertical wrap fills the first column completely before starting the second, so item 2 sits below item 1. Masonry sends each item to whichever column is shortest at that moment, so item 2 starts the second column. Item 2 is highlighted because its position is the whole difference: with items of equal height all three arrangements would look the same, which is why the confusion survives.

reading.text: The grid is a different promise
"Objects in a grid don't wrap to the next line." A grid places children into cells; it does not flow them along an axis and break when they run out of room.

In exchange, grid children can span rows or columns — a hero cell two columns wide above four single-column cells, held in one structure. Rows and columns can be resized. This is the flow for layouts whose shape is the point: a dashboard, a pricing table, a bento arrangement where certain cells are deliberately bigger than others.

So the choice is a question about intent. Do these items form a sequence that should reflow when space changes — a row of tags, a list of messages, a set of cards? Use a wrapping horizontal or vertical flow. Do they occupy positions in a structure that should survive a resize — a grid of tiles where the big one stays big? Use the grid. Reaching for the grid because a layout looks grid-shaped is the common error; what matters is whether the arrangement is a sequence or a structure.
Auto layout is available on all plans and needs edit access to the file. In Figma Slides and Figma Buzz it works in design mode and requires a Full seat.
The words for these parts

items.def: The direction the flow runs. Set by flex-direction in CSS; by the flow you pick in Figma.
Perpendicular to the main axis. Where a row flows across, the cross axis runs down the columns.
The frame with auto layout on it, and its direct children. Only direct children are items.
One row or column of a wrapped flow. MDN suggests treating each line as a new container.
The main axis runs along the row, in the inline direction.
The main axis runs in the block direction, top to bottom.
Children continue onto a new line when they run out of room. Off by default in CSS, where the initial value is nowrap.

items.as: — no CSS or Figma equivalent here
items.def: Items packed into whichever column is shortest, so no rows form. Neither auto layout flow does this.

reading.text: Take any screen you use daily and find one group of repeating elements — a tag list, a nav, a row of cards. Decide, before you touch Figma, whether it is a sequence or a structure. Then build it with the flow your answer implies, add two more items than it was designed for, and narrow the frame until it reflows. If the arrangement collapses into something nonsensical, you chose the wrong flow — which is the point of the exercise.

cards.front: Which auto layout flows support wrap?
cards.back: Horizontal and vertical only. The grid does not wrap — its children occupy cells.

cards.front: What does wrap produce in a vertical flow?
cards.back: A new column. Explicitly not a masonry layout — it fills one column, then starts the next.

cards.front: What can grid children do that children of a wrapping flow cannot?
cards.back: Span rows or columns. Rows and columns can also be resized.

cards.front: When you apply auto layout, how does Figma choose the flow?
cards.back: It guesses from how the objects are already arranged, and you can switch flow at any time.

quiz.question: You need a tag list that continues onto a second line as tags are added and as the frame narrows. Which flow?
options: Grid, because the tags form rows
Horizontal with wrap enabled
Vertical with wrap enabled
Any flow — wrap is a frame-level setting independent of flow
quiz.why: A tag list is a sequence that should reflow, which is what horizontal wrap does — it continues onto a new row. A grid would hold the tags in fixed cells instead of letting them flow, and vertical wrap would produce columns.

quiz.question: A designer sets a vertical flow to wrap, expecting a Pinterest-style ragged arrangement. What do they get?
options: A masonry layout, which is what vertical wrap is for
Columns — items fill one column, then start the next
An error; vertical flows cannot wrap
Rows, because wrap always produces rows
quiz.why: Vertical wrap fills a column and starts another. The documentation states outright that it is not a masonry layout, because the expectation is common enough to need correcting — masonry packs items of differing heights into the shortest slot, and nothing in auto layout does that.

exact.prompt: How many auto layout flows does Figma offer?
exact.note: Vertical, horizontal and grid. Only the first two can wrap.

exact.prompt: CSS property that sets which way a flex container's main axis runs
exact.note: row and column in CSS; horizontal and vertical in Figma.

items: Distinguish padding from gap and say which belongs to the parent
Use the three distribution options available to an automatic gap
Explain why both values should be variables rather than numbers

reading.text: Two numbers govern the space inside an auto layout frame, and confusing them is the most common beginner error in Figma. Padding is "the empty or white space between the edge of a parent auto layout frame and its objects." Gap is the space between the objects themselves. Padding belongs to the container; gap belongs to the arrangement.

The practical consequence is where you go to fix something. If a card's contents are crowding its border, that is padding, and you change it on the card. If the contents are crowding each other, that is gap, and you change it on the same frame but in a different field. Designers who have not internalised the distinction tend to fix a padding problem by adding a spacer layer, which works once and then breaks every time the content changes.
Padding has three levels of control

items: Uniform — one value on all four sides.
Per axis — one value vertically, another horizontally.
Per side — top, right, bottom and left set independently.

reading.text: Most components want per-axis. A button with equal padding on all four sides looks wrong, because optical balance in a horizontal control wants more room on the left and right than above and below. Per-side is for the cases where something genuinely is asymmetric: a panel with a flush edge, a card whose image bleeds to the top.
Gap can be automatic

Gap takes a number, or it takes Auto — in which case the available space is divided for you, with three distributions to choose between: Between, Around and Evenly. Between puts all the space between the items and none at the ends, which is what a navigation bar wants when its links should reach both edges. Around and Evenly distribute space to the ends too, in different proportions.

Automatic gap is how you get a layout that stays correct at two widths without a second variant. It is also how you get a layout that drifts, if you apply it to something whose spacing was meant to be fixed. The test is whether the space between items carries meaning: in a nav bar it does not, so let it stretch. In a form, the space between a label and its field is a relationship, and it should be a number.
Both values accept variables

Padding and gap can both be bound to number variables rather than typed as literals. This is the hinge that connects this chapter to design tokens later in the course: once spacing is a variable, changing one value in one collection restyles every frame that consumes it, and switching a mode re-spaces an entire file. A layout built from literals cannot do that, and retrofitting it means visiting every frame.
Build the habit now, before the course reaches variables: when you type a spacing number more than twice, it wants to be a variable.
The words for these parts

items.def: Equal space between items and none at the ends: “the first item is flush with the main-start edge, and the last item is flush with the main-end edge.”
The space before the first and after the last item “equals half of the space between each pair of adjacent items.”
Every gap is the same, ends included — items get “a full-size space on either end.”
Space between the parent frame's edge and its objects. Same word in both places.
Space between the objects. Figma and CSS use the same word; CSS also has row-gap and column-gap separately.

reading.text: Build a card with per-axis padding and a fixed gap. Then duplicate it and rebuild the duplicate using Auto gap with Between. Put both in a frame and narrow it. Watch which one keeps its internal rhythm and which one stretches — then write down, in a sentence, which behaviour each of your real components wants.

cards.front: Padding versus gap — which is which?
cards.back: Padding is the space between the parent frame's edge and its objects. Gap is the space between the objects. Padding belongs to the container, gap to the arrangement.

cards.front: The three distributions available to an automatic gap
cards.back: Between, Around and Evenly. Between places space only between items; the other two also give space to the ends.

cards.front: Why should padding and gap be variables rather than typed numbers?
cards.back: Both accept number variables, so one edit in a collection re-spaces every frame that consumes it — and a mode switch can re-space a whole file. Literals have to be visited one by one.

quiz.question: A nav bar's links should reach both edges of the bar with equal space between them, at any width. What produces that?
options: A fixed gap and fill-container on each link
Auto gap with the Between distribution
Auto gap with the Evenly distribution
Per-side padding set to zero on left and right
quiz.why: Between puts all available space between the items and none at the ends, so the first and last link sit flush against the padding. Evenly would also pad the ends, pulling the outer links inward.

quiz.question: A card's text is touching the card's border. Which value is wrong?
options: The gap, because the text is too close to something
The padding on the card
The text layer's own resizing mode
The gap on the parent of the card
quiz.why: Distance from the container's edge is padding by definition. Gap governs distance between siblings, so it cannot move a child away from the frame's border.

exact.prompt: Which automatic gap distribution puts space only between items and none at the ends?
exact.note: The other two, Around and Evenly, both give space to the ends as well.

exact.prompt: CSS value equivalent to Figma's Between distribution
exact.note: Equal gaps between items, none at the ends — the first and last sit flush against the edges.

lessons.title: Hug, Fill, Fixed — and the Min/Max Pair

items: Say which resizing modes apply to a parent and which to a child
Predict a frame's width from its contents and padding
Combine a minimum or maximum with another resizing mode

reading.text: Resizing is set per axis, through the width and height fields, and it is the property that decides whether a layout survives contact with real content. There are three modes and two constraints, and the thing worth memorising is not what they are called but what each one attaches to.
What attaches to what

items: Hug contents — applies to auto layout frames. The frame resizes based on its children.
Fill container — applies to children of auto layout frames. The object fills the available space.
Fixed width or height — applies to both. The size stays as set.
Minimum width or height — applies to both. The size is equal to or greater than the minimum.
Maximum width or height — applies to both. The size is equal to or less than the maximum.

reading.text: Hug is a parent's answer to the question "how big am I?" — it defers to its children. Fill is a child's answer to the same question — it defers to its parent. An object cannot hug unless it contains something, and it cannot fill unless something contains it. Most layout confusion in Figma is a hug applied where a fill was wanted, or the reverse, and naming which direction the deference runs resolves it immediately.
Arithmetic worth doing once

A text layer 40 pixels wide, inside a frame with 10 pixels of padding on the left and right, produces a 60-pixel frame. Grow the text to 50 pixels and the frame becomes 70. That is the entire mechanic of hug: the frame is the sum of its contents and its padding, recomputed whenever either changes. A button built this way fits its label in every language; a button built at a fixed 120 pixels fits its label in one.

Typing a number into the width field is itself a mode change — enter 125 and the resizing becomes Fixed width. This catches people out: they nudge a value to check something, and silently convert a flexible frame into a rigid one. If a layout stopped reflowing and you cannot see why, check whether something that should hug has quietly become fixed.
Minimum and maximum are additive, not alternative

Min and max are added explicitly — Add min width, Add max width, Add min height, Add max height — and removed just as explicitly with Remove min and max. They combine with the other resizing settings rather than replacing them, which is what makes them useful: a child set to fill its container, with a minimum width of 80 pixels, stretches with the layout until the layout gets small, and then refuses to shrink below something legible.

Maximum does the opposite job and is how you stop a text column from running to 1,400 pixels on a wide monitor. Both accept a number variable, which means the breakpoint at which your layout stops stretching can itself be a token.

The success test for this chapter is the one Figma's own materials set: change a button's label or resize the frame, and everything reflows correctly. If anything needs manual repair afterwards, something is fixed that should hug or fill.
The words for these parts

items.def: Sizes from the children. MDN: max-content is “the intrinsic preferred width”; fit-content uses “the available space, but not more than max-content.”
Sizes from the parent. MDN describes stretch as setting the element's margin box to the width of its containing block.
A literal size that ignores both children and parent.
Floors and ceilings that combine with the mode above rather than replacing it.
What an element wants to be. MDN's example: max-content is as wide as the text, min-content as wide as the widest word.

reading.text: Build a card: image, heading, body, and a row of two buttons. Set every container to hug and every child that should stretch to fill. Give the card a minimum width of 280 and a maximum of 480. Now drag its width from 200 to 900 pixels and watch. Then change the heading to something three times longer. Nothing should need touching — and if it does, note which layer it was, because that is the one whose resizing mode you guessed wrong.

cards.front: Hug contents — what does it apply to, and what does it do?
cards.back: Auto layout frames. The frame resizes based on its child objects — it defers to its contents.

cards.front: Fill container — what does it apply to, and what does it do?
cards.back: Children of auto layout frames. The object fills all available space — it defers to its parent.

cards.front: A 40px text layer with 10px of left and right padding. How wide is the hugging frame?
cards.back: 60px. Grow the text to 50px and the frame becomes 70px — the frame is its contents plus its padding.

cards.front: What happens when you type a number into the width field of a hugging frame?
cards.back: The resizing mode changes to Fixed width. Typing a value is a mode change, which is how flexible frames silently become rigid.

cards.front: Do minimum and maximum dimensions replace the other resizing modes?
cards.back: No — they combine with them. Fill plus a minimum width stretches with the layout but refuses to shrink below the minimum.

quiz.question: Which resizing mode can only be applied to a child object of an auto layout frame?
options: Hug contents
Fill container
Fixed width
Minimum width
quiz.why: Fill is a child's deference to its parent, so it needs a parent. Hug is the mirror image and applies to auto layout frames; fixed, min and max apply to both.

quiz.question: A text column stretches to the full width of a 1,600px monitor and becomes unreadable. The column is set to fill its container. What is the minimal fix?
options: Change it to fixed width at a readable size
Add a maximum width to the column
Add a minimum width to the column
Change the parent from hug to fixed
quiz.why: A maximum combines with fill: the column keeps stretching with the layout until it reaches the cap, then stops. Switching to fixed would also cap it, but would break the stretching at every width below the cap too.

quiz.question: A card stopped reflowing when its heading got longer, and nothing obvious changed. What should you check first?
options: Whether the heading's font has variable axes
Whether a frame that should hug has become fixed
Whether the gap is set to Auto
Whether the card is a component instance
quiz.why: Typing any value into a width or height field converts that axis to Fixed, and it is easy to do by accident while checking a dimension. A fixed parent cannot grow to fit a longer child.

exact.prompt: A 40px text layer with 10px padding on left and right. Width of the hugging frame, in pixels?
exact.note: Contents plus padding. Grow the text to 50px and the frame becomes 70px.

exact.prompt: Which resizing mode makes a frame size itself from its children?
exact.note: Its mirror image is fill container, which sizes a child from its parent.

exact.prompt: CSS width value that means “as wide as the content prefers”
exact.note: MDN calls it “the intrinsic preferred width”. min-content is as wide as the widest word.

lessons.title: Ignore, Nest, and the Constraint Rule

items: Take an object out of the auto layout flow deliberately
State the rule governing constraints inside an auto layout frame
Nest auto layout frames without losing control of spacing

reading.text: Auto layout positions every child along its flow. Sometimes you need one that is not positioned that way — a badge pinned to a card's corner, a close button in the top right, a gradient overlay covering the whole frame. The escape hatch is Ignore auto layout, which "was formerly known as absolute position" and works "much like absolute position in CSS." The object stays a child of the frame, but the flow stops arranging it.

The old name is worth knowing because it is still what most tutorials, most team conversations and most of your own muscle memory will call it. The rename is an improvement — the object is not absolutely positioned in any coordinate system, it is simply excluded from a flow — but the concept is the CSS one.
The rule that explains a whole class of confusion
"You can't apply constraints to child objects in an auto layout frame, unless the object ignores the auto layout flow."

This resolves the question every designer asks in their first month: why are the constraint controls greyed out? Because constraints and auto layout are two answers to the same question, and an object can only have one. Constraints say "stay this far from that edge as the parent resizes." Auto layout says "take your position from the flow." An object cannot do both, so inside an auto layout frame the flow wins — until you ignore it, at which point constraints become available and the badge you pinned to the corner stays in the corner.

The inverse case is permitted and useful: an auto layout frame nested inside a plain frame can take constraints. The auto layout governs the frame's insides; the constraints govern where the frame sits in its parent. Nothing conflicts, because the two rules apply at different levels.
Nesting

"Nesting refers to the act of placing a layer inside of another layer," and nested auto layout frames each keep their own padding and gap. This is how real interfaces are built: a card is a vertical flow containing a horizontal flow for its header, a text block, and another horizontal flow for its buttons. Four frames, four independent spacing contexts, one structure that reflows as a unit.

The discipline that makes nesting survivable is naming. A file with nine layers called Frame 427 is unmaintainable regardless of how well it reflows, and nesting multiplies the problem — you cannot select the right layer if you cannot tell them apart. Nesting structure also travels: it is what a component's internals are made of, what smart animate matches between frames, and what an agent reads when you hand it a file.
The words for these parts

items.def: MDN: “removed from the normal document flow, and no space is created for the element in the page layout.” Figma's docs make the same comparison.
What an absolutely positioned element is measured from — “the ancestor relative to which the element is positioned.” In Figma that is the frame you ignored the flow inside.
The arrangement an element participates in until something removes it. Auto layout is Figma's normal flow.
“The act of placing a layer inside of another layer.” Each nested auto layout frame keeps its own padding and gap.
How a non-flowed child keeps its distance from an edge as the parent resizes.

reading.text: Build a card with a badge pinned to its top-right corner, and make the card's width drag from 240 to 600 pixels with the badge staying put. You will need Ignore auto layout, and then a constraint. Then try the same thing without ignoring the flow, and observe exactly which controls are unavailable — that greyed-out panel is the rule in this chapter made visible.

cards.front: Ignore auto layout — what was it formerly called, and what is it like?
cards.back: Formerly absolute position. It works much like absolute position in CSS: the object stays a child of the frame but is excluded from the flow.

cards.front: Why are constraint controls unavailable on a child of an auto layout frame?
cards.back: Constraints and auto layout both answer "where does this sit as the parent resizes," and an object can only have one answer. Ignoring the flow makes constraints available.

cards.front: Can an auto layout frame itself have constraints?
cards.back: Yes, when it is nested inside a plain frame. Auto layout governs its insides; constraints govern where it sits in its parent.

cards.front: What happens to padding and gap when auto layout frames are nested?
cards.back: Each nested frame keeps its own padding and gap — independent spacing contexts inside one reflowing structure.

quiz.question: You need a notification badge pinned to the top-right corner of a card whose width changes. What is required?
options: Set the badge to fill container and align it right
Set the badge to ignore auto layout, then apply a constraint
Nest the badge in its own auto layout frame with right alignment
Give the card per-side padding to reserve the corner
quiz.why: Constraints are what pin something to an edge across a resize, and they are only available to a child that has been taken out of the flow. Alignment within a flow positions relative to siblings, not to a corner.

quiz.question: Which of these is permitted?
options: Constraints on a child object inside an auto layout frame, with the flow active
Constraints on an auto layout frame nested inside a plain frame
Auto layout and constraints both governing the same object's position
Constraints on every child of a grid flow
quiz.why: The two rules apply at different levels, so nothing conflicts: the auto layout arranges the frame's contents while the constraints place the frame inside its own parent.

exact.prompt: What was Ignore auto layout formerly called?
exact.note: Still what most tutorials and team conversations call it. The documentation compares it to absolute position in CSS.

exact.prompt: CSS position value that Ignore auto layout corresponds to
exact.note: Removed from normal flow and measured from its containing block.

lessons.title: Where Auto Layout Meets Everything Else

items: Predict what an instance can and cannot change about its auto layout
Apply the two text rules that break fluid layouts
Explain why naming consistency matters to smart animate

reading.text: Auto layout does not live alone. It meets components, prototypes and text, and each meeting has a documented friction point. These are the places real files break, and all four are stated plainly in the documentation — which means there is no excuse for discovering them the hard way.
Components
"You will need to add auto layout to each component individually. There isn't currently a way to add auto layout in bulk."

Plan for that before building fifty components, not after. It is also a strong argument for getting the structure right in a small kit first: whatever you got wrong, you will fix one component at a time.

An instance is more restricted than its main component, and the restrictions are specific. An instance may adjust padding and gap. It may not reorder layers, and it may not add new ones. Deleting a layer in an instance only hides it — the layer is still there, which is why a hidden layer can reappear when the main component changes.

Read that list as a design brief rather than a limitation. If a component needs to be used with its layers in a different order, that is not an instance override, it is a variant or a slot. The restrictions tell you where the seams in your component API have to be.
Prototypes

Smart animate matches objects between frames and animates the difference — but it "do[es] not take into account the background of a frame," so a transition that appears to change a background will not animate it. Scrolling needs content that genuinely extends past the frame's bounds; a frame whose contents hug will never scroll, because there is nothing to scroll to. Presentation view supports scrolling long frames by default.

Because smart animate matches objects, it depends on those objects being recognisably the same across frames — which makes naming consistency load-bearing rather than tidy. Rename a layer between two frames and the transition stops seeing them as the same thing, and the smooth morph becomes a cut.
Text
"Text layers cannot have both a max height and a set number of max lines." Adding a max height sets max lines to Auto; setting max lines removes the max height.

They are two ways of saying the same thing — stop after this much — and the tool refuses to hold both, because they would disagree the moment the font size changed. Pick the one that matches your intent: max lines when the constraint is editorial (a card shows two lines of summary), max height when it is spatial (this region is 96 pixels tall whatever is in it).

And the standing advice, for anyone building layouts meant to be fully fluid: the documentation "advise[s] against using fixed size text boxes." A fixed text box is a promise that the content will never change length, which is a promise no interface keeps — not across languages, not across a CMS, not across a product decision made after you shipped.

Take a component you have already built and try to break it in four documented ways: reorder an instance's layers, delete a layer in an instance and then change the main, set both a max height and max lines on a text layer, and smart-animate between two frames where one layer has been renamed. Write down what actually happened in each case. You now know the four failure modes by having caused them, which is the only way they stay known.

cards.front: Can auto layout be applied to several components at once?
cards.back: No. It has to be added to each component individually — there is currently no bulk way.

cards.front: What can an instance change about its auto layout, and what can't it?
cards.back: It can adjust padding and gap. It cannot reorder layers or add new ones, and deleting a layer only hides it.

cards.front: What does smart animate not take into account?
cards.back: The background of a frame. A transition that looks like it changes a background will not animate it.

cards.front: Why is naming consistency load-bearing for prototypes?
cards.back: Smart animate matches objects between frames to animate the difference. Rename a layer and it stops being recognised as the same object, so the morph becomes a cut.

cards.front: Max height and max lines on a text layer — can you set both?
cards.back: No. Adding a max height sets max lines to Auto; setting max lines removes the max height. They are two statements of the same constraint.

quiz.question: A layer was deleted in an instance. Later the main component is updated and the layer reappears. Why?
options: The update reset all instance overrides
Deleting in an instance only hides the layer; it was never removed
The instance was detached and re-attached
Hidden layers always reappear on publish
quiz.why: Instances cannot remove layers — the delete is a hide. The layer remains part of the instance's structure, so a change to the main component can bring it back into view.

quiz.question: A long frame will not scroll in the prototype. Its contents are set to hug. What is wrong?
options: Scrolling must be enabled in Presentation view
Hugging means nothing extends past the frame's bounds, so there is nothing to scroll
Smart animate overrides scroll behaviour
Scroll requires the grid flow
quiz.why: Scroll overflow needs content that genuinely extends past the frame. A frame sized to hug its contents is exactly as tall as them, so there is no overflow to scroll through.
quiz.key: nothing extends past the frame's bounds

quiz.question: You are building a layout intended to be fully fluid across languages and breakpoints. Which practice does the documentation advise against?
options: Nesting auto layout frames more than three deep
Using fixed size text boxes
Applying min and max to the same axis
Using Auto gap with the Between distribution
quiz.why: A fixed text box asserts that the content will never change length. Across languages and content changes that assertion fails, and the layout breaks at exactly the point it was supposed to flex.

exact.prompt: In an instance, deleting a layer actually does what?
exact.note: Which is why a hidden layer can reappear when the main component changes.

items: Place any design number in one of three tiers: normative, platform guidance, or convention
State the WCAG minimums you can actually be wrong about
Answer “why 16?” in a review without bluffing

reading.text: Sooner or later someone asks why the padding is 16 and not 12, and the quality of the answer is most of the impression you leave. There are standards in this work, but far fewer than the internet implies, and the useful skill is not memorising numbers — it is knowing which tier a number belongs to. Three tiers, with very different force.
Tier one: the numbers with force

WCAG is the only tier that is normative. It is a W3C Recommendation, it is what accessibility legislation points at, and AA is the level nearly all of that legislation targets. These are the numbers where you are not unconventional but wrong.
SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA: “The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when:”

items.def: At least 24 by 24 CSS pixels.
At least 44 by 44 CSS pixels. The 2.5.8 page suggests aiming for it “for important links/controls” — a best practice, not a requirement.
4.5:1 for text; 3:1 for large-scale text.
3:1 “against adjacent color(s)” for information needed to identify components and states, and for parts of graphics needed to understand content.

reading.text: Two details that catch people out. Large-scale text is defined, not estimated: “at least 18 point or 14 point bold,” which the specification itself converts — “1pt = 1.333px, therefore 14pt and 18pt are equivalent to approximately 18.5px and 24px.” And the thresholds are hard: “the computed values should not be rounded (e.g., 4.499:1 would not meet the 4.5:1 threshold).”

The exceptions are part of the standard rather than loopholes in it, and knowing them is what separates compliance from box-ticking. A target may be under 24px when it is inline — “in a sentence or its size is otherwise constrained by the line-height of non-target text” — when an equivalent control elsewhere meets the rule, when the user agent determines the size and the author does not modify it, or when the presentation is essential. Logotypes have no contrast requirement at all. There is also a spacing route: undersized targets pass if “a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle” centred on each does not intersect another target.
This app holds itself to 2.5.8 and goes past it: 24px is the floor everywhere, raised to 44px wherever the pointer is actually coarse. A compliance minimum is not a comfortable thumb.
Tier two: platform guidance, which is not a standard

Apple and Google both publish numbers for their own platforms. They are authoritative there and carry no force anywhere else — and their own language admits it. Material says: “For most platforms, consider making touch targets at least 48 x 48dp,” and separately “Consider making pointer targets minimums 44 x 44dp.” Note the verb. Material advises; WCAG requires.

Material also makes the point this chapter is built on, about the gap between what a control looks like and what it is: “an icon may appear to be 24 x 24dp, but the padding surrounding it comprises the full 48 x 48dp touch target.” The visible mark and the hit area are different objects, which is exactly the trick this app uses for its own citation markers.

And now the honest part, because it is more instructive than a number. The famous rule that Apple requires 44 by 44 points is not something I could find Apple stating. Searching the current Human Interface Guidelines pages for Layout, Accessibility and Buttons, the only 44 that appears is a visionOS button size token — “Regular (44 pt)”, one of five sizes beside Mini, Small, Large and Extra large. No minimum tap target is stated on any of those three pages.

Where does the number in this chapter come from, then? From Google. Material's accessibility page carries the line “Note: iOS recommends 44 x 44dp targets.” The most-repeated figure in mobile design reaches you here via a competitor's documentation. It may well be stated somewhere in Apple's materials; the point is that almost nobody citing it has checked, and a designer who says “Apple's minimum is 44” in a review is repeating something they cannot source. “WCAG AA requires 24, and Material suggests 48” is both more useful and verifiable.
Tier three: conventions that get called standards

The 8-point grid is the most-cited standard in interface design and it is not a standard at all. Material's own Grids & spacing page states no pixel or dp value whatsoever. What it says is that spacing “helps group content, direct attention, and shape the personality of a product.” Personality. The vendor most associated with the 8dp grid describes spacing as expression, and leaves the number to you.

That does not make the convention worthless — a consistent step of 4 or 8 removes a decision from every layout and makes a file legible to anyone who joins it, which is reason enough. It makes it a convention, adopted because it is useful, not obeyed because it is correct. Modular type scales are the same: the Figma agent offered a minor third as one ratio among several, describing it as “balanced, versatile for most projects.” A recommendation with alternatives is not a rule.

Corner radius has no standard anywhere in this material, and I went looking. Across every source behind this course the words corner and radius appear only in discussions of screen corners as unbounded Fitts targets and of blast radius in AI safety. Nothing suggests a correct roundness, because there isn't one. Radius is brand: sharp corners read as precise and institutional, generous ones as soft and consumer, and both are right for someone. It is one of the few numbers in interface design that is purely a choice — which is why it is the first thing a brand changes and the last thing a standard will ever specify.
The test to apply

From the HCI course, chapter 16: “a design system's specifications are findings rather than opinions: minimum touch target sizes are Fitts and motor precision, contrast floors are perception and accessibility research, motion durations come from the object-constancy work.”

Run every number in your system through that sentence. A specification is a finding, a platform's advice, or a choice. 24 by 24 is a finding and a requirement. 48dp is advice. 8-pixel spacing is a convention you adopted. 12-pixel radius is a choice you made. All four are legitimate; stating which is which is what makes you sound like someone who knows, and refusing to dress a choice as a finding is the whole of the professional difference.

So when the question comes — why 16 and not 12 — the credible answer is not a citation. It is “our spacing step is 8, so 16 is two steps; the control it sits in has to clear 24 by 24 regardless, and it does.” One convention, one requirement, and no pretending the convention is the requirement.

Open any screen you have designed and list eight numbers from it — paddings, radii, font sizes, target sizes, durations. Against each, write finding, advice or choice, and for anything you called a finding, name the source. Then check every interactive element against 24 by 24 CSS pixels and see how many pass. The list you cannot source is the list you cannot defend in a review.

cards.front: The three tiers a design number can belong to
cards.back: Normative (WCAG, referenced by legislation), platform guidance (Apple, Material — authoritative for their platform only), and convention (8-point grids, type ratios, radius).

cards.front: SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) — value and level
cards.back: At least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, Level AA. The enhanced version, 2.5.5, asks for 44 by 44 at AAA.

cards.front: How does WCAG define large-scale text?
cards.back: At least 18 point, or 14 point bold — which the spec converts to approximately 24px and 18.5px at 1pt = 1.333px.

cards.front: Why is the 8-point grid not a standard?
cards.back: No normative document states it. Material's own Grids & spacing page gives no value at all and describes spacing as shaping “the personality of a product”. It is a useful convention, not a rule.

cards.front: What is the standard for corner radius?
cards.back: There isn't one. It is a brand choice — the only tier-three number that is purely expressive, which is why no standard will ever specify it.

cards.front: The difference between a visible control and its target
cards.back: They are separate objects. Material: “an icon may appear to be 24 x 24dp, but the padding surrounding it comprises the full 48 x 48dp touch target.”

quiz.question: In a design review someone asks why your buttons are 44px tall. Which answer is most defensible?
options: “44 is Apple's minimum tap target.”
“WCAG AA requires 24 by 24; we use 44 because the pointer is coarse and Material suggests at least 48 for touch.”
“It's the industry standard for mobile buttons.”
“Our 8-point grid makes 44 the nearest valid step.”
quiz.why: It separates the requirement from the advice and cites both accurately. The Apple claim is the one almost nobody can source — the number reaches most designers through Material's note about iOS, not through Apple. And 44 is not a multiple of 8, so the last answer is also false.
quiz.key: WCAG requires 24; the rest is advice

quiz.question: A contrast check returns 4.499:1 on body text. What is the status under SC 1.4.3?
options: Passes — it rounds to 4.5:1
Fails — computed values are not rounded
Passes if the text is 18px or larger
Passes at AA, fails at AAA
quiz.why: The understanding document is explicit: “the computed values should not be rounded (e.g., 4.499:1 would not meet the 4.5:1 threshold).” It would only pass as large-scale text, which needs 18pt or 14pt bold — roughly 24px or 18.5px bold, not 18px regular.

quiz.question: Which of these is a target-size exception that genuinely exists in SC 2.5.8?
options: Targets inside a scrollable container
A target in a sentence, constrained by the line-height of surrounding text
Any target on a desktop-only layout
Targets smaller than 16 by 16 CSS pixels
quiz.why: The Inline exception covers a target “in a sentence or its size is otherwise constrained by the line-height of non-target text” — a link inside a paragraph cannot be padded out without wrecking the paragraph. The other three are invented.

exact.prompt: Minimum target size under WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8, in CSS pixels (one number)
exact.note: Level AA. The enhanced criterion 2.5.5 asks for 44 by 44, but that is AAA and described as a best practice to consider.

exact.prompt: Contrast ratio required for body text at WCAG AA
exact.note: Large-scale text needs 3:1. Values are not rounded — 4.499:1 fails.

exact.prompt: Touch target size Material suggests for most platforms, in dp (one number)
exact.note: “Consider making touch targets at least 48 x 48dp” — advice, not a requirement. For pointers it suggests 44.

exact.prompt: Which WCAG success criterion number governs non-text contrast?
exact.note: 3:1 against adjacent colours, for anything needed to identify a component or its state.
